consensus_summary: Storm/tempest primarily symbolizes divine judgment/wrath and theophanic power over chaos, or else the trials/tribulations of life (or the Church) that Christ stills; chaos, eschatological national upheaval, and related motifs appear as common alternatives.
book_summary: The nations in turmoil, imaged as the raging sea that is stilled at Christ’s word “Peace, be still.”
consensus_core_identification: Divine judgment/theophany or life’s trials/adversities mastered by God/Christ
book_core_identification: Nations in turmoil (raging sea stilled by Christ)
boundary_disagreement: Book limits the symbol to national/political turmoil (equated with roaring seas) and re-centers the stilling-of-the-storm texts on that national referent, thereby de-emphasizing or excluding the broader personal-trial and pure-judgment applications that dominate the consensus.
material_contradiction: None; national turmoil is already present inside the consensus’s chaos/judgment/eschatological alternatives and is compatible with divine mastery over the sea.
rationale: Minimum cores share the same general category—overwhelming chaotic force under divine control—drawn from overlapping texts (stilling pericopes, prophetic tempests, seas as peoples). Consensus treats the category polyvalently with primary weight on judgment or personal trials; the book preserves that category while narrowing its extension and precision to the specific case of nations, as its printed verses (Ps 65:7; Isa 17:12-13; Luke 21:25) and cross-reference to Sea & Waters make explicit. This is boundary refinement, not replacement of the central referent.
strongest_objection: Consensus (especially pastoral/devotional strands) privileges personal trials via the Gospel boat stories or general prophetic judgment; making “nations in turmoil” the core may be seen as an over-specific reclassification that sidelines those dominant readings.
